title: Aurora Kitchen: should it enter the UK?
prompt: Aurora Kitchen is a US maker of premium frozen meals. It sells only in North America. Its board is considering launching in the UK and has asked for your recommendation on whether to go ahead. All figures in this case are in pounds. How would you approach this?

facts.answer: Aurora sells premium and organic frozen meals in US supermarkets. It has strong recipes and a well-known US brand but has never operated outside North America.
The board wants an annual operating profit of at least £5m within three years of launch, and the entry investment paid back within three further years.
Aurora would launch only its premium range, through UK supermarkets, run by a small UK-based team. A UK contract manufacturer would make the products.
The one-off entry investment is £15m (launch marketing, supermarket listing fees and set-up). It is spent before sales start.
Once launched, the UK business has fixed costs of £6m a year (team, marketing and distribution overhead). These do not change with sales volume.
UK frozen ready-meal sales are split into three segments: family meals, single-serve meals, and premium and organic. Aurora would compete only in premium and organic.
Three established UK premium brands hold about 60% of the premium segment. Supermarket own-label ranges hold roughly another 25%.
If the launch goes well, Aurora expects 6% of the premium segment by year three.
UK shoppers are used to premium own-label ranges priced below branded products. Aurora would price in line with the leading premium brands.
UK labelling rules differ slightly from US rules. The contract manufacturer would handle compliance.
Aurora has no UK retailer relationships and no UK supply chain, and would need cold-chain distribution.

key_buckets: Market attractiveness: size, growth and segments
Competition: who holds share and how Aurora would differentiate
Ability to win: brand, product fit, retailer access, supply chain
Economics: revenue, margins, fixed costs, investment and payback
good_signs: Frames the decision around the board's profit and payback targets
Segments the market and focuses on the segment Aurora would actually enter
Builds the profit estimate step by step from market size to payback
Tests what would have to be true (for example, the share needed to break even)
red_flags: Treats the whole £2bn frozen-meal market as Aurora's market
Discusses only the market and ignores Aurora's own economics
Gives a recommendation without using the numbers

exhibits.title: UK frozen ready-meal market by segment (£ million)
exhibits.reveal_hint: Ask for the size and growth of the UK market and its segments.
exhibits.insight: Premium and organic is the smallest segment today (£400m) but the fastest growing: up 25% over three years, against about 6% for family meals and about 9% for single-serve.

exhibits.title: Aurora UK variable cost per £1 of revenue (pence)
exhibits.reveal_hint: Ask about Aurora's costs and margins in the UK.
exhibits.insight: Variable costs are 60p per £1 of revenue, so gross margin is 40%. Cold-chain logistics is the largest cost after ingredients.

math.question: At 6% of the premium and organic segment in year 3, what is Aurora's UK revenue, in £ million?
What is the gross profit on that revenue, in £ million?
math.working: Variable cost is 60p per £1, so gross margin is 40%. 40% of £30m is £12m.

math.question: After the £6m of fixed costs, what is the annual operating profit in year 3, in £ million?
math.working: £12m gross profit minus £6m fixed costs is £6m.

math.question: At that annual profit, how many years does it take to pay back the £15m entry investment?

brainstorm.question: What could Aurora do to improve its chances in the UK or reduce the risk of entering?
idea_bank: Partner with a UK distributor that already runs cold-chain delivery
Launch with one retailer or one region first, then expand if targets are met
Adapt flavours and recipes to UK tastes
Test demand online or in a small store trial before the full investment
Price slightly below the leading premium brands to win initial trial
Acquire or partner with a small UK premium brand to gain shelf access
Hire a UK leader with supermarket buying experience
Use the contract manufacturer to avoid building a factory
Stage the £15m so that spending is released as milestones are hit

must_mention: The premium segment is attractive: growing about 25% to £500m
At 6% share the economics work: about £6m annual profit and a 2.5-year payback
The main risk is winning 6% share against established brands and own-label
good_signs: Tests sensitivity: at 3% share, revenue is £15m, gross profit £6m and profit is zero
Recommends a staged entry with clear milestones
Names concrete next steps such as retailer conversations and a pilot

model_answer_outline: Clarify the objective: at least £5m annual operating profit within 3 years of launch, and payback of the £15m within 3 further years.
Structure: market attractiveness, competition, Aurora's ability to win, economics, entry mode and risks.
Market: premium and organic is the smallest segment (£400m today) but fastest growing, to £500m by year 3 (+25%).
Economics: 6% share is £30m revenue; 40% gross margin gives £12m; after £6m fixed costs, £6m profit; payback is 15 / 6 = 2.5 years.
Sensitivity: at 3% share the business only breaks even, so winning share is the key uncertainty.

Recommendation: enter, but staged. Start with one supermarket partner and a UK cold-chain distributor, release the £15m against share milestones, and decide on a full roll-out after 12 months of sales data.
